newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe faces strikes on EMU - German labour boss.
newsitem.headline: Europe faces strikes on EMU - German labour boss.

text.p: One of Germany's most powerful trade union officials has warned that Europe faces strikes and social unrest as anger rises over austerity measures being introduced by governments ahead of economic and monetary union in 1999.

Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the Confederation of German Trade Unions (DBG), said European governments were wrong to try to force through such drastic budget cuts at a time of rising unemployment across the continent.

"We need EMU. But it depends how it is shaped. If it is done the way (German finance minister Theo) Waigel wants it,...then there is the risk of huge strikes," Engelen-Kefer told a briefing of international journalists in Bonn late on Wednesday.
Waigel is one of the most outspoken advocates of strict adherence to the public debt and deficit criteria that countries must satisfy by 1997 for entry into EMU two years later.

But Engelen-Kefer, whose DGB organisation represents some nine million union members across Germany, said the cuts being made to welfare and social security systems meant that the poorest in society were suffering the most.

"The cost-cutting should not mean that you take money out of the pockets of the little man," she said, adding that accompanying measures to stimulate the job market or protect existing positions were necessary.
Unemployment in Europe is currently riding at around 11 percent, double that in the United States.
Efforts by trade unions and left-leaning politicians to introduce employment policies into the Maastricht Treaty for currency union have so far proved unsuccessful.

In Germany, where the jobless total pushed further above the four million level in November, new laws designed to slash 70 billion marks ($45 billion) from public spending next year have already sparked a wave of protests by citizens and workers.
The laws, passed by parliament in September, included reforms to Germany's comfortable health and pension systems and included cuts to sick pay entitlements and a relaxation of job protection law.

The sick pay cuts in particular have led to a deterioration of labour relations and triggered protests by workers across German industry, led by hundreds of thousands of workers in the key metal and engineering sector.

Engelen-Kefer said that, rather than attempting to meet the Maastricht criteria by reducing social costs, the German government and others would do better to follow the Italian example of increasing revenues through a "euro tax".
"It would be much more intelligent to have a special tax for Maastricht," she said.
